findings.reason: a worker sent at `reckon/crew/merge.py` finds nothing to remove and closes on a guarantee the module already holds, while the path that staged the source and forced five hours of refusals stays unfixed.
findings.text: §24's Why says "the merge verb brings a run's head into the primary checkout and then decides whether the landing may stand ... staged its four files there and was then refused", but the module the section names builds the merge out of objects and never stages a head's files in the checkout: `merge.py`'s own docstring (`reckon/crew/merge.py:1-19`) states the design and `land_merge` (`reckon/crew/merge.py:1375-1500`) runs a caller's refusal in the `verify` seam before the branch moves, with the merge computed by `merge-tree --write-tree` and committed by `commit-tree`, then moved by `git merge --ff-only`; `reckon/crew/merge.py` contains no `git add`, `checkout` or `read-tree` at all, and only one index write, the `restore --staged --source=HEAD` of already-landed paths at `reckon/crew/merge.py:751` — so the write-then-refuse ordering the repair is aimed at is absent from that module and the actor that staged the incident's four files, and left the shared checkout dirty, is unnamed

findings.reason: without a base arm that fails, the gate cannot show any guard fires, and every arm in the section passes on the unfixed code.
findings.text: §24's negative control, "at the base revision the refused merge leaves the head's files staged and the second merge is refused", cannot reproduce, because at the base revision that verb's refusals all occur before the branch moves and it writes no working-tree or index change (the `verify` seam at `reckon/crew/merge.py:1480` and the `--ff-only` move at `:1484`), so the base arm passes and the section's whole measure rests on a case that holds however the code behaves

findings.reason: the arm the incident's own defect class produces (unreviewed source nobody's head explains) is untested and the deliverable leaves its obligation content undecided, so two implementations can both pass while disagreeing on the checkout's most common dirty state.
findings.text: §24's obligation clause covers "staged or modified product source that matches no commit on the primary branch" but requires the obligation to name "the run whose head they match", which is undefined for precisely the population the first clause names (a hand edit matching no run), and the second case at `plan.html:197` exercises only source that matches a run's older head, so an implementation that raises nothing when no run matches passes every arm

findings.reason: the preset module list is what sends the node at a verb that cannot produce the incident, so removing it and stating the records (a restored index and working tree at the touched paths; one obligation naming paths and the run) leaves the worker to find the path that actually stages source.
findings.text: §24 closes "Write paths: `reckon/crew/merge.py`, `reckon/crew/obligations.py` and `tests/test_a_refused_merge_restores_the_checkout.py`", naming the modules to change and the test file to add rather than the records and figures the section delivers, which fixes a guess about the code in plan text; here the guess is also the one the root-cause finding shows is wrong, since the first named module already holds the restoration guarantee
